questions.q: The product of an object's mass and its velocity is referred to as its momentum, p. Which statement correctly describes momentum and its units?
options: Momentum is a scalar quantity measured only in joules
Momentum is a vector quantity, measured in either newton seconds (N s) or in kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹)
Momentum is a vector quantity measured in newtons (N)
Momentum is the product of force and time, measured in metres per second
questions.explanation: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity. It is a vector quantity (it has the same direction as the velocity) and is measured in either newton seconds (N s) or kilogram metres per second (kg m s⁻¹).

questions.q: Which statement best expresses the Law of Conservation of Momentum for two colliding objects?
options: For any closed isolated system, the sum of the momenta of all objects in that system is a constant, so the total momentum after a collision equals the total momentum before
The momentum of the faster object is always conserved while the slower object gains all the energy
Momentum is conserved only when the colliding objects bounce apart, not when they stick together
The sum of the momenta increases during a collision because forces are applied
questions.explanation: The Law of Conservation of Momentum states that for any closed isolated system the sum of the momenta of all objects is a constant. So the sum of the momenta of the objects after a collision equals the sum of the momenta before the collision.

questions.q: The actual change in momentum of an object, Δp, is also referred to as its impulse. Which set of relationships for impulse is correct?
options: Δp = mΔv only, and impulse cannot be found from force
Δp = m(v − u) = FΔt, so impulse can be found either from the change in velocity or from the force and the time interval over which it acts
Δp = F/Δt, so a longer time gives a larger impulse for the same force
Δp = ½mv², the kinetic energy of the object
questions.explanation: The change in momentum (impulse) of an object can be found from its mass and change in velocity, Δp = mΔv = m(v − u). Because F = ma and a = (v − u)/Δt, this also equals FΔt — the force acting on the object multiplied by the time interval over which it acts.

questions.q: A putter exerts a force of 8 N for a time interval of 0.01 s on a golf ball at rest on the green. With what velocity will the ball leave the putter if the ball has a mass of 50 g?
questions.explanation: Apply the impulse relationship FΔt = m(v − u) with u = 0. The putter gives the ball a velocity of 1.6 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A 2000 kg delivery van collides with a small stationary car of mass 1000 kg. The two vehicles lock together and the tangled wreck moves off at 20 m s⁻¹ in the direction the van was travelling. At what speed was the van travelling just before it hit the small car?
working: By conservation of momentum \(\Sigma p_{after} = \Sigma p_{before} = m_{van}u_{van} + m_{car}u_{car}\)
questions.explanation: The wreck's momentum after impact is (2000 + 1000) × 20 = 60 000 kg m s⁻¹. Since the stationary car contributes no momentum before, all of that came from the van, so u_van = 60 000 / 2000 = 30 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: When a moving billiard ball strikes a stationary one, kinetic energy may be transferred between the colliding objects. In a perfect collision no energy is lost in the form of sound, heat or elastic potential energy. What is such a collision called, and what happens in a real (inelastic) collision?
options: An inelastic collision; in such a collision all of the kinetic energy is transferred and none is lost

An elastic collision; in a real inelastic collision some of the original kinetic energy is converted into other forms such as sound and heat, so the transfer of kinetic energy is incomplete, although momentum is still conserved
A perfectly inelastic collision; in an elastic collision the colliding objects always stick together
An elastic collision; in an inelastic collision momentum is not conserved while kinetic energy is conserved
questions.explanation: In a collision kinetic energy may be transferred between the colliding objects. A perfect collision, in which no energy is lost in the form of sound, heat or elastic potential energy and kinetic energy is conserved, is an elastic collision. The vast majority of real collisions are inelastic: momentum is conserved regardless, but some of the original kinetic energy is converted into other forms such as sound and heat, so the transfer of kinetic energy is incomplete.

questions.q: From memory, summarise the difference between an inelastic collision and an elastic collision, and state in how many dimensions momentum is conserved.
keyPoints: An inelastic collision is one in which only momentum is conserved.
An elastic collision is one in which both kinetic energy and momentum are conserved.
Momentum is conserved in one-, two- and three-dimensional collisions.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that an inelastic collision conserves only momentum, that an elastic collision conserves both kinetic energy and momentum, and that momentum is conserved in one-, two- and three-dimensional collisions, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Cars are designed to crumple at the front and rear. In terms of momentum and force, how does a crumple zone protect occupants in a collision?
options: It reduces the change in momentum of the occupants to zero so no force acts
It increases the time interval during which the momentum of the car and its occupants changes, which reduces the net force on the occupants
It increases the force on the occupants so the car stops faster
It conserves the kinetic energy of the occupants by storing it in the crumpled panels
questions.explanation: A crumple zone increases the time interval during which the momentum of the car changes in a collision. For a fixed change in momentum, increasing the time interval reduces the net force on the occupants — the same impulse principle used by airbags, seatbelts and helmets.

questions.q: From memory: why is total momentum conserved in a collision? Explain using Newton's third law.
keyPoints: During the collision object A pushes on object B, and by Newton's third law B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force.
The two objects are in contact for the same length of time, so each experiences that force for the same duration.
Impulse is force times time, so A and B receive equal and opposite impulses — equal and opposite changes in momentum that cancel, leaving the total momentum of the system unchanged.
questions.explanation: The proof is: equal and opposite forces (Newton's third law) acting for the same contact time give equal and opposite impulses, so the changes in momentum cancel. If you named the third law, the equal contact time and the cancelling impulses, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: A 70 kg person jumps and lands, changing their momentum by 420 kg m s⁻¹ as they stop. Explain, using impulse, why bending the knees on landing reduces the risk of injury. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The change in momentum on landing is fixed at 420 kg m s⁻¹ regardless of how the person lands. Since impulse equals force times time and also equals the change in momentum (Δp = FΔt), the force depends on the time over which the momentum change occurs: F = Δp/Δt. Bending the knees increases the time taken to stop, so for the same change in momentum the average force is reduced, lowering the risk of injury. This is the same principle as airbags and crumple zones — extend the time, cut the force.

criteria.descriptor: States the change in momentum is fixed regardless of how the person lands.
Relates impulse to force and time (Δp = FΔt), so F = Δp/Δt.
Concludes that increasing the stopping time reduces the average force, lowering injury risk.

questions.explanation: The crux is that the change in momentum is set by the situation, so spreading it over a longer time lowers the peak force — exactly the airbag and crumple-zone principle.
